attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his essay, stating his own view of Klarna.

semantics.note: Retrospective observation. The proposition leaves out 'hyping them proudly for quite some time', but the contract covers that element. Otherwise faithful.

contract.note: Reading a hiring freeze plus touted AI-driven headcount cuts as 'AI layoffs', and a CEO admission of lower quality plus rehiring as 'realized they screwed up', is an ordinary reading. 'Among the first' has no exact benchmark, so it is judged by prominence and timing.

evidence.note: Dec 2024 report: the CEO touts an AI-driven hiring freeze since 2023 and the 700-agent claim. This shows sustained public hype.
The 2024 700-agent announcement moved Teleperformance shares. This marks Klarna as a prominent early case.
May 2025: the CEO says the cost focus led to lower quality and pivots to investing in human support.
The walkback was partial: AI-driven shrinkage continued. This qualifies the claim but does not negate the admission.
Published before the evaluation date. Most US AI-attributed cuts came in 2025, after Klarna's 2023–24 claims. This bears on timing but covers other firms.

reviews.rationale: Klarna publicly touted AI-driven staff reductions in 2023–24, before the 2025 wave of AI-attributed cuts. In May 2025 its CEO admitted the cost push had lowered quality and said Klarna was hiring humans again. The walkback was partial, and there is no exact ranking of who reversed first, but the claim holds on the contract's fair reading.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion. He paraphrases Hinton only as the premise, and the claim scored is Marcus's own observation.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'to my knowledge' qualifier and the 2016 premise. 'To my knowledge' limits the scope to documented knowledge; it is not a probability hedge.

contract.note: Reading 'not one' as 'no documented AI displacement' fits the stated hedge. Workforce, residency and vacancy data are reasonable measures.

evidence.note: Confirms Hinton's 2016 statement, which is part of the contract's support condition.
Record US radiology residency positions in 2025 and all-time-high vacancies.
AI has stayed mostly assistive over the decade; radiologist headcounts and salaries kept rising.
May 2025 report: Mayo Clinic radiologist staff grew about 55% since 2016 despite heavy AI use.

reviews.rationale: Hinton's 2016 statement is confirmed. By 2025, radiology residency positions, vacancies, headcount and salaries had all risen, and the packet shows no documented AI-driven radiologist job cuts. The evidence is US-centred and not a global census, but that fits the claim as hedged by 'to my knowledge'.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. They follow his agreement with Garman, but this sentence is his own assertion.

semantics.note: A general capability observation. 'Often' describes frequency, not probability, so the claim is firm and scoreable on a plain reading.

contract.note: Using end-to-end project completion and quality versus experts as proxies for junior work and senior judgement is an ordinary reading, though imperfect: no benchmark tests job seniority or judgement directly. Calendar 2025 is a reasonable period.

evidence.note: RLI, Oct 2025: the best agent automated only 2.5% of real projects end to end. AI often cannot do the whole job.
GDPval: the best model won or tied on about 48% of tasks against experts. It does some of the work and falls short on the rest.
GDPval tasks come from professionals averaging 14 years' experience. This links the benchmark to senior work.

reviews.rationale: 2025 benchmarks show AI matching experienced professionals on about half of tasks but falling short on the rest, and completing only about 2.5% of real projects end to end. That fits 'some but often not all' and 'often lacks' expert-level quality on the contract's fair proxy reading.
